questions.title: Mockito Fundamentals
questions.question: How do you use Mockito effectively for unit testing?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Mock`: creates mock, `@InjectMocks`: injects mocks into class under test**
- **`when(...).thenReturn(...)` for stubbing, `verify(...)` for interaction verification**
- **`@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`: JUnit 5 integration**
- **`@Spy`: partial mock — real object with some methods stubbed**
- **`ArgumentCaptor`: capture argument to assert on it later**
- **Red flag:** using `@MockBean` in pure unit tests — that's for Spring integration tests

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Mockito is the standard Java mocking framework. You create mock objects with `@Mock`, and Mockito injects them into the class under test with `@InjectMocks`. When you call `when(mock.method()).thenReturn(value)`, Mockito stubs the mock to return the specified value when that method is called.

After the act phase, you verify that expected interactions happened using `verify(mock).method(argument)`. `ArgumentCaptor` is useful when you can't easily verify the argument inline — you capture it and assert separately.

`@Spy` is for partial mocking: a real object where you override only specific methods. Use spies when the class has real behavior you want to keep but need to stub one or two expensive operations.

questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock
questions.question: What is the difference between @MockBean and @Mock and when should you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Mock` (Mockito): no Spring context — pure unit test**
- **`@MockBean` (Spring Test): replaces a bean in Spring context — integration test**
- **`@MockBean` is slow: starts Spring context, then replaces beans**
- **Use `@Mock` for unit tests — fast, no context overhead**
- **Use `@MockBean` with `@WebMvcTest` or `@SpringBootTest` — Spring controls wiring**
- **Red flag:** using `@MockBean` in simple service tests — unnecessary context startup

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Mock` is a pure Mockito annotation — it creates a mock object that you manually inject (via `@InjectMocks` or constructor). No Spring application context is loaded. Tests run in milliseconds. This is what you use for unit tests.

`@MockBean` is a Spring Test annotation that registers a mock as a Spring bean in the application context, replacing any real bean of the same type. This is only meaningful when you're loading a Spring context with `@WebMvcTest` or `@SpringBootTest`. It's significantly slower because the context must start.

The common pattern with `@WebMvcTest`: the test slice loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, converters). Services and repositories are not included — you provide them as `@MockBean` so the controller can be wired up.
